focus: Exodus 2 answers Pharaoh’s decree with the birth and rescue of Moses, then follows him from Pharaoh’s house to a failed attempt to defend his people and a long exile in Midian. The chapter closes by turning from Moses to Israel’s cry under bondage and to God, who hears, remembers His covenant, and sees His people.

sections.title: Moses Is Hidden, Drawn from the River, and Raised as Pharaoh’s Daughter’s Son
sections.summary: A Levite mother hides her son for three months, places him in an ark of bulrushes among the reeds, and his sister watches from a distance. Pharaoh’s daughter has compassion on the Hebrew child, pays his own mother to nurse him, and names him Moses, “Because I drew him out of the water” (Exodus 2:10).

sections.title: Moses Kills an Egyptian and Flees from Pharaoh
sections.summary: Grown to manhood, Moses goes out to his brethren, kills an Egyptian who is beating a Hebrew, and hides him in the sand. The next day a Hebrew rejects him with “Who made you a prince and a judge over us?” (Exodus 2:14), and when Pharaoh seeks to kill him, Moses flees to Midian and sits down by a well.

sections.title: Moses Finds a Home in Midian
sections.summary: At the well Moses defends the seven daughters of the priest of Midian and waters their flock, and their father Reuel welcomes him to eat bread. Moses settles there, marries Zipporah, and names his son Gershom, saying, “I have been a stranger in a foreign land” (Exodus 2:22).

sections.title: God Hears Israel’s Groaning and Remembers His Covenant
sections.summary: The king of Egypt dies, but Israel’s bondage continues, and their cry goes up to God. God hears their groaning, remembers “His covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob” (Exodus 2:24), looks upon the children of Israel, and acknowledges them.

1.brief: A man from the house of Levi marries a daughter of Levi. The story of Israel’s deliverer begins quietly with an ordinary Levite household living under Pharaoh’s decree.
1.explain:
“And a man of the house of Levi went and took as wife a daughter of Levi.”

The story of Israel’s deliverer begins quietly. “A man of the house of Levi” marries “a daughter of Levi.” Neither is named here. Later we learn that the father was Amram and the mother Jochebed (6:20). For now the focus falls on an ordinary Levite household living under Pharaoh’s decree that every newborn son be thrown into the river (1:22).

God often begins His great works in ways that look small. No one watching would have guessed that a baby born to this couple would lead Israel out of Egypt.
1.notes:
Numbers 26:59 names the mother as Jochebed, “the daughter of Levi who was born to Levi in Egypt,” and lists Aaron, Moses, and Miriam as her children.

Aaron was three years older than Moses (7:7). The sister of 2:4 was also older than Moses.

2.brief: The woman bears a son, and seeing that he is a beautiful child, she hides him for three months. Her hiding the baby defies Pharaoh’s order, and Hebrews 11:23 credits the parents’ action to faith.
2.explain:
“So the woman conceived and bore a son.”

Under Pharaoh’s decree, the birth of a son meant mortal danger.

“And when she saw that he was a beautiful child, she hid him three months.”

The mother “saw that he was a beautiful child.” The word “beautiful” translates the ordinary Hebrew word for “good.” It recalls how God saw that His creation was good (Genesis 1). She saw something special in this child.

So “she hid him three months.” Hiding the baby defied Pharaoh’s order. Hebrews credits the parents’ action to faith: “By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden three months by his parents, because they saw he was a beautiful child; and they were not afraid of the king’s command” (Hebrews 11:23).
2.notes: Stephen says Moses “was well pleasing to God” (Acts 7:20). Stephen’s wording echoes the Greek translation of Exodus 2:2, which uses the same Greek word that Stephen uses where the NKJV of Exodus has “beautiful.”

3.brief: When she can no longer hide him, she makes an ark of bulrushes, seals it with asphalt and pitch, and lays the child in it among the reeds by the river’s bank. The river Pharaoh meant for the death of Hebrew sons becomes the place where this son is protected.
3.explain:
“But when she could no longer hide him,”

A baby grows louder and harder to hide. After three months, “she could no longer hide him.” She had to find another way to protect him.

“she took an ark of bulrushes for him, daubed it with asphalt and pitch,”

She made “an ark of bulrushes,” a small basket woven from papyrus reeds. She “daubed it with asphalt and pitch,” sealing it with tar to keep out the water. The word “ark” is the same Hebrew word used for Noah’s ark (Genesis 6:14). In both stories, God preserves life through an ark sealed with pitch as waters threaten.

“put the child in it, and laid it in the reeds by the river’s bank.”

She placed the basket at the river’s edge. The reeds along the edge of the Nile would keep the basket from floating away. The river Pharaoh meant for the death of Hebrew sons becomes the place where this son is protected.
3.notes:
The Hebrew word for “ark” appears only in the stories of Noah and of Moses. A different word is used for the ark of the covenant.

The word translated “reeds” is the same word used in the phrase often translated “Red Sea,” which can be rendered Sea of Reeds (for example, 13:18).

4.brief: The child’s sister stands at a distance to see what will happen to him. Her watchfulness prepares for the part she will play when he is found.
4.explain:
“And his sister stood afar off, to know what would be done to him.”

The baby’s “sister” stayed nearby. She “stood afar off,” close enough to watch but far enough not to draw attention. She waited “to know what would be done to him.” The text does not name her here. She is most likely Miriam, who later appears as Moses’ sister and as a prophetess (15:20; Numbers 26:59). Her watchfulness prepares for the part she will play when he is found.

5.brief: Pharaoh’s daughter comes down to the river to bathe, sees the ark among the reeds, and sends her maid to bring it. The rescue of the child begins in the household of the king who ordered his death.
5.explain:
“Then the daughter of Pharaoh came down to bathe at the river.”

“The daughter of Pharaoh” came to the river “to bathe.” The rescue of the Hebrew child begins in the household of the king who ordered his death.

“And her maidens walked along the riverside;”

Her “maidens,” her attendants, walked along the bank while she bathed.

“and when she saw the ark among the reeds, she sent her maid to get it.”

She “saw the ark among the reeds” and “sent her maid to get it.” Her curiosity brought the basket to her hands. Behind what looks like chance stands the God who watches over His people.
5.notes: The text does not name Pharaoh’s daughter. Later traditions gave her various names, but Scripture does not.

6.brief: When she opens the ark and sees the baby crying, she has compassion on him and says, “This is one of the Hebrews’ children.” She recognizes the child as one of the Hebrews under her father’s decree and still responds with compassion.
6.explain:
“And when she opened it, she saw the child, and behold, the baby wept.”

She “opened it” and “saw the child.” At that moment “the baby wept.” The cry of a helpless infant reached her.

“So she had compassion on him,”

She felt pity for the crying baby. Compassion moved her before policy did.

“and said, ‘This is one of the Hebrews’ children.”

She knew at once what she was looking at: “This is one of the Hebrews’ children.” She understood that this was one of the boys her father had ordered drowned. She recognized the child as one of the Hebrews under her father’s decree and still responded with compassion.

7.brief: The child’s sister boldly offers to find a Hebrew nurse for Pharaoh’s daughter. Her question opens the way for the baby to be returned to his own family.
7.explain:
“Then his sister said to Pharaoh’s daughter,”

The watching sister stepped forward and spoke “to Pharaoh’s daughter.” It was a bold move for a slave girl to address a princess.

“Shall I go and call a nurse for you from the Hebrew women, that she may nurse the child for you?”

She offered to find “a nurse for you from the Hebrew women.” A baby needed a nursing mother. A Hebrew woman could nurse the child for the princess. Her question opens the way for the baby to be returned to his own family.
7.notes: In the ancient world it was common for wealthy women to hire a wet nurse. Contracts for wet nurses have survived from the ancient Near East.

8.brief: Pharaoh’s daughter says, “Go,” and the girl goes and calls the child’s own mother. The sister’s proposal is accepted, and the baby is about to be returned to the woman who hid him.
8.explain:
“And Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, ‘Go.”

Pharaoh’s daughter gave a one-word answer: “Go.” The sister’s proposal was accepted.

“So the maiden went and called the child’s mother.”

The sister did not bring a stranger. She brought the baby’s own mother. The woman who had hidden him and placed him in the river would now hold him again.
8.notes: The Hebrew word translated “maiden” describes a young woman of marriageable age or younger. It suggests that the sister was a girl, not a small child.

9.brief: Pharaoh’s daughter tells the mother to take the child and nurse him, and promises to pay her wages. The mother is paid to raise her own son in safety, an outcome no one in Israel could have arranged.
9.explain:
“Then Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, ‘Take this child away and nurse him for me, and I will give you your wages.”

Pharaoh’s daughter told the mother, “Take this child away and nurse him for me.” The princess claimed the child as hers, but she gave him back to his mother to raise. She even promised, “I will give you your wages.” The mother would be paid to care for her own son.

“So the woman took the child and nursed him.”

The baby who had been condemned to death now lived safely in his own home, under the protection of Pharaoh’s own daughter. No one in Israel could have arranged such an outcome. God turned Pharaoh’s decree upside down.
9.notes: Children in the ancient world were often nursed until about two or three years old (compare 1 Samuel 1:22–24). Moses likely spent his earliest years with his own family.

10.brief: When the child is grown, his mother brings him to Pharaoh’s daughter, he becomes her son, and she names him Moses, “Because I drew him out of the water.” The name remembers how he was rescued, and he now enters Pharaoh’s own household.
10.explain:
“And the child grew, and she brought him to Pharaoh’s daughter, and he became her son.”

“The child grew.” When he was weaned, his mother “brought him to Pharaoh’s daughter,” and “he became her son.” Moses was adopted into Pharaoh’s household. Stephen says he “was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians” (Acts 7:22). The future deliverer of Israel was raised in the palace of Israel’s oppressor.

“So she called his name Moses, saying, ‘Because I drew him out of the water.”

Pharaoh’s daughter “called his name Moses.” She explained, “Because I drew him out of the water.” The name remembers how he was rescued. It also points ahead. The one drawn out of the water would one day draw Israel out of Egypt and through the waters of the sea.
10.notes: The name Moses sounds like the Hebrew verb meaning to draw out. It also resembles an Egyptian word meaning “son” or “born,” found in Egyptian names. The narrator connects it with the Hebrew verb.

11.brief: When Moses is grown, he goes out to his brethren, sees their burdens, and sees an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, “one of his brethren.” Though raised in Pharaoh’s house, Moses identifies with the oppressed Hebrews as his own people.
11.explain:
“Now it came to pass in those days, when Moses was grown,”

The story jumps ahead. “When Moses was grown,” he was a man. Stephen says he was about forty years old (Acts 7:23).

“that he went out to his brethren and looked at their burdens.”

Moses “went out to his brethren.” Though raised as an Egyptian prince, he knew who his people were. He “looked at their burdens,” seeing their forced labor with his own eyes. The verb suggests more than a glance. He looked with concern.

“And he saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his brethren.”

What he saw was violence against one of his own people. The narrator stresses that the man being beaten was “one of his brethren.” Moses identified with the oppressed Hebrews as his own people. Hebrews says Moses chose “to suffer affliction with the people of God” rather than enjoy the pleasures of Egypt (Hebrews 11:24–26).
11.notes: The Hebrew verb translated “beating” is the same verb translated “killed” in 2:12. The Egyptian struck the Hebrew, and Moses struck the Egyptian.

12.brief: Moses looks this way and that, and seeing no one, kills the Egyptian and hides him in the sand. The text records the killing and its concealment without commending it, and the secrecy shows Moses acting on his own initiative.
12.explain:
“So he looked this way and that way, and when he saw no one,”

Before acting, Moses “looked this way and that way.” He checked to see if anyone was watching. “When he saw no one,” he acted. The secrecy shows that Moses knew what he was doing would be seen as a crime.

“he killed the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.”

He struck the man down and buried the body.

The text records the killing and its concealment without commending it. Moses was moved by real concern for his people, and Stephen says he expected Israel to understand that God would deliver them by his hand (Acts 7:25). But Moses acted on his own initiative, in secret, and by violence. God had not yet sent him. The LORD would commission him forty years later at the burning bush.

13.brief: The next day Moses sees two Hebrews fighting and asks the one in the wrong why he is striking his companion. He tries to make peace among his own people, as he tried to defend them the day before.
13.explain:
“And when he went out the second day, behold, two Hebrew men were fighting,”

“The second day,” Moses went out again. This time he saw “two Hebrew men” fighting each other. Israel’s problems were not only with Egypt. They also fought among themselves.

“and he said to the one who did the wrong, ‘Why are you striking your companion?”

Moses spoke “to the one who did the wrong.” He tried to make peace: “Why are you striking your companion?” He tried to make peace among his own people, as he tried to defend them the day before.
13.notes: The Hebrew word translated “the one who did the wrong” describes the guilty party, the one in the wrong.

14.brief: The man replies, “Who made you a prince and a judge over us?” and asks whether Moses means to kill him as he killed the Egyptian. Moses’ own people reject his leadership, and he realizes in fear that his deed is known.
14.explain:
“Then he said, ‘Who made you a prince and a judge over us?”

The man shot back, “Who made you a prince and a judge over us?” He rejected Moses’ authority. Moses had no recognized right to rule or judge them.

“Do you intend to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?”

His second question exposed what Moses had done in secret. The secret was out. Moses’ own people reject his leadership.

“So Moses feared and said, ‘Surely this thing is known!”

“Moses feared.” He realized, “Surely this thing is known!” If one Hebrew knew, others did too, and word would reach Pharaoh. His deed was no longer hidden.

Stephen draws out the meaning: Moses’ own people “did not understand” that God would deliver them by his hand, and they pushed him away (Acts 7:25–27, 35).

15.brief: When Pharaoh hears of it, he seeks to kill Moses, and Moses flees to the land of Midian and sits down by a well. His first attempt to help his people ends in exile, and the well sets the scene for his new life.
15.explain:
“When Pharaoh heard of this matter, he sought to kill Moses.”

“Pharaoh heard of this matter.” He “sought to kill Moses.” The adopted grandson of Pharaoh was now a wanted man.

“But Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh and dwelt in the land of Midian;”

“Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh.” He escaped and went to “the land of Midian,” a region east of Egypt, generally placed in northwest Arabia or the Sinai peninsula. The Midianites were descendants of Abraham through Keturah (Genesis 25:1–2).

“and he sat down by a well.”

His first attempt to help his people ended in exile. The well sets the scene for his new life. In Genesis, wells were places where marriages began: Abraham’s servant found Rebekah at a well (Genesis 24), and Jacob met Rachel at a well (Genesis 29).
15.notes: Hebrews says Moses left Egypt “not fearing the wrath of the king” (Hebrews 11:27). Interpreters differ on whether Hebrews refers to this flight or to the later exodus, since Exodus 2:14 says Moses was afraid.

16.brief: The priest of Midian has seven daughters, who come to draw water and fill the troughs for their father’s flock. The setting introduces the household that will become Moses’ home.
16.explain:
“Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters.”

“The priest of Midian” is introduced. He “had seven daughters.” His name is given in 2:18 as Reuel, and elsewhere as Jethro (3:1). As a priest, he was a leading figure in his community.

“And they came and drew water, and they filled the troughs to water their father’s flock.”

The daughters “came and drew water.” They “filled the troughs to water their father’s flock.” Drawing water from a well was hard work, and the daughters had done it.
16.notes: The text does not say what god the priest of Midian served. Later he blesses the LORD and offers sacrifices to God (18:10–12).

17.brief: Shepherds drive the daughters away, but Moses stands up, helps them, and waters their flock. Even in exile Moses acts to defend the weak against those who mistreat them.
17.explain:
“Then the shepherds came and drove them away;”

After the daughters had done the work of drawing water, other shepherds pushed them aside to use the water for their own flocks.

“but Moses stood up and helped them, and watered their flock.”

“But Moses stood up.” He “helped them,” driving off the shepherds. Then he “watered their flock.” Even in exile, Moses acted to defend the weak against those who mistreated them. The same concern for justice that moved him in Egypt moved him here.
17.notes: The Hebrew verb translated “helped” is the word usually translated “save” or “deliver.” The daughters use a different verb in 2:19, “delivered.” Moses acts as a deliverer for these women before he becomes Israel’s deliverer.

18.brief: When the daughters return home, their father Reuel asks why they have come back so soon. His question opens the way for the story of the Egyptian who helped them to be told.
18.explain:
“When they came to Reuel their father, he said,”

The daughters went home to “Reuel their father.” The name Reuel is usually understood to mean friend of God. He is also called Jethro (3:1; 18:1).

“How is it that you have come so soon today?”

Reuel noticed that his daughters were home early. His question suggests that the shepherds usually drove his daughters away and made them wait. His question opens the way for the story of the Egyptian who helped them to be told.
18.notes: The relationship among the names Reuel, Jethro, and Hobab (Numbers 10:29) is debated. Reuel and Jethro most likely name the same man, Moses’ father-in-law.

19.brief: The daughters explain that an Egyptian delivered them from the shepherds and even drew water and watered the flock. They identify Moses as an Egyptian, and they credit him with both rescuing them and doing their work.
19.explain:
“And they said, ‘An Egyptian delivered us from the hand of the shepherds,”

The daughters explained: “An Egyptian delivered us from the hand of the shepherds.” They called Moses “an Egyptian.” His clothing, speech, or appearance marked him as Egyptian. They did not know he was a Hebrew.

“and he also drew enough water for us and watered the flock.”

He also did the work they had come to do. He did more than rescue them. He did their work. They credited him with both rescuing them and doing their work.

20.brief: Reuel asks where the man is, rebukes his daughters for leaving him, and tells them to invite him to eat bread. The hospitality of this Midianite household opens a door for the exiled Moses.
20.explain:
“So he said to his daughters, ‘And where is he? Why is it that you have left the man?”

Reuel asked, “And where is he?” He rebuked his daughters: “Why is it that you have left the man?” In that culture, failing to offer hospitality to someone who had helped you was shameful.

“Call him, that he may eat bread.”

Reuel invited Moses to a meal. “Eat bread” means to share a meal. The hospitality of this Midianite household opens a door for the exiled Moses.

21.brief: Moses is content to live with Reuel, who gives him his daughter Zipporah as his wife. The fugitive from Pharaoh settles into a new family in Midian.
21.explain:
“Then Moses was content to live with the man,”

He agreed to stay. The fugitive found a home.

“and he gave Zipporah his daughter to Moses.”

Reuel gave Moses one of his daughters in marriage. The fugitive from Pharaoh settled into a new family in Midian.

22.brief: Zipporah bears a son, and Moses names him Gershom, saying, “I have been a stranger in a foreign land.” The name expresses Moses’ own sense of being an outsider, far from both Egypt and his people.
22.explain:
“And she bore him a son. He called his name Gershom,”

Zipporah “bore him a son.” Moses “called his name Gershom.”

“for he said, ‘I have been a stranger in a foreign land.”

Moses explained the name: “I have been a stranger in a foreign land.” The name sounds like the Hebrew word for “stranger.” It expresses Moses’ own sense of being an outsider, far from both Egypt and his people. He had been a Hebrew in Egypt, and now he was an Egyptian-raised Hebrew in Midian. He belonged fully to neither place.
22.notes:
The name Gershom sounds like the Hebrew word for “stranger” or “sojourner.” Moses’ second son, Eliezer, is named in 18:4.

Some Greek manuscripts add an account of a second son here, but the Hebrew text does not.

23.brief: In the course of time the king of Egypt dies, but Israel’s bondage continues, and the people groan and cry out because of it. Their cry rises to God, and the story turns from Moses in Midian back to the suffering people in Egypt.
23.explain:
“Now it happened in the process of time that the king of Egypt died.”

“In the process of time” marks a long period. Stephen says Moses spent forty years in Midian (Acts 7:30). During that time “the king of Egypt died.” The Pharaoh who sought to kill Moses was gone.

“Then the children of Israel groaned because of the bondage, and they cried out;”

But Israel’s situation did not improve. “The children of Israel groaned because of the bondage.” The new king continued the oppression. They “cried out,” calling for help.

“and their cry came up to God because of the bondage.”

“Their cry came up to God.” Their groaning was not lost. It reached the God of their fathers. The story turns from Moses in Midian back to the suffering people in Egypt.
23.notes: The text does not say that Israel prayed to God, only that they groaned and cried out. Their cry nevertheless “came up to God.”

24.brief: God hears their groaning and remembers “His covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.” To remember here means that God now turns to act on the promises He made to the fathers.
24.explain:
“So God heard their groaning,”

The cry that rose from Egypt reached God’s ears. This is the first of four verbs in these closing verses that describe God turning toward His people.

“and God remembered His covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.”

God does not forget. To remember here means that God now turns to act on the promises He made to the fathers. He had promised Abraham that his descendants would be afflicted in a foreign land, but that He would judge that nation and bring them out (Genesis 15:13–14). That time has come.
24.notes: The covenant with Abraham is recorded in Genesis 12:1–3; Genesis 15:1–21; and Genesis 17:1–21. God confirmed it to Isaac (Genesis 26:2–5) and to Jacob (Genesis 28:13–15; 35:11–12).

25.brief: God looks upon the children of Israel and acknowledges them. The chapter closes with God fully attentive to His people’s suffering, which prepares for His appearance to Moses at the bush.
25.explain:
“And God looked upon the children of Israel, and God acknowledged them.”

“God looked upon the children of Israel.” He saw their suffering. “God acknowledged them.” He took notice of them, recognized their condition, and took it to heart.

The chapter closes with God fully attentive to His people’s suffering. God heard, remembered, looked, and acknowledged. The next chapter shows what His attention leads to: He appears to Moses at the bush and says, “I have surely seen the oppression of My people” and “I know their sorrows” (3:7).
25.notes: The Hebrew text of the last clause reads literally and God knew. The NKJV renders it “acknowledged them.” The Greek translation reads and He made Himself known to them.
